en: The horizontal axis is the share people want, the vertical axis is the resulting segregation. The higher above the dashed line (y=x), the more separated it ended up than people wanted.

What it shows: Each individual holds only a mild wish, "I don't want to be a minority," yet together these choices can produce strong separation that nobody wanted. The shape of the group can differ from what individuals intended.

What it doesn't show: It doesn't mean real residential segregation is all due to this. Housing prices, school districts, jobs and discriminatory policies are not in this model. Also, if the "desired share" is set too high (60% or more), there is almost no arrangement that satisfies everyone, and people just keep moving.

Original model: Thomas C. Schelling (1971), "Dynamic Models of Segregation", Journal of Mathematical Sociology 1(2). This implementation is the common variant: a 50×50 grid with wrap-around edges, 8 neighbors, and moving to a random empty cell.
A person with no neighbors at all counts as content. In each round, unhappy people move one at a time in random order.
Graph ③ changes only the desired share on the same layout and runs up to 100 rounds; if no arrangement satisfies everyone, it measures the state at that point.
The code is available on GitHub.
Why Do Sunflower Seeds Sit at That Angle? · Simulatio Lab
Change the turning angle as seeds are placed one by one, and see which angle fills the disc evenly with no gaps.
Why do sunflower seeds grow around at about 137.5 degrees per step? Change the angle you turn as each seed is placed, and check which angle fills the disc evenly without gaps.
The k-th seed sits √k away from the center, turned a fixed angle further than the previous seed. This arrangement is called phyllotaxis (Vogel's spiral).
When the angle is close to a simple fraction of 360° (90° is 1/4, 120° is 1/3, 144° is 2/5), seeds pile up along the same directions, leaving spokes and large gaps.
The golden angle (about 137.508°) divides 360° in the golden ratio, and is known as the angle farthest from any simple fraction.

Packing quality is measured by taking many points on the disc and finding the distance to the nearest seed; the mean (average gap) and the maximum (largest gap) are divided by the ideal spacing. Smaller means more evenly filled. In "Color by", coloring by the remainder after dividing the seed number by something like 34 reveals the spiral arms.

① Watching the Sunflower Grow
Seeds are added one at a time. Change the angle and watch how the pattern differs. Near the golden angle there are almost no gaps, while angles like 120° or 144° produce spokes.
② How Big Are the Gaps at Each Angle?
The horizontal axis is the angle between seeds, the vertical axis is the average gap (log scale). Most angles stay similarly low, but near simple fractions of 360° the gap spikes sharply.
③ Comparing Special Angles
Compares the average gap of a few angles at the current seed count. Lower means more evenly filled, and gold is the golden angle.
④ Distance to the Nearest Neighbor
The distribution of the distance from each seed to its nearest neighbor at the current angle. Even spacing gives one sharp peak; overlap or sparse spots spread it out.

What it shows: With 600 seeds, the golden angle (137.508°) has an average gap of 0.38, and only 0.3% of the angles from 90° to 180° (scanned in 0.1° steps) scored lower. Angles near simple fractions such as 90°, 120°, 144° and 180° score 2.4 to 5.0, which is 6 to 13 times worse. The evenness of spacing (coefficient of variation of neighbor distances) is 0.012 at the golden angle, while 137.7°, off by only 0.2°, gives 0.107, about 9 times less even. At the golden angle, the index difference between close neighbors is a Fibonacci number (55 and 34 with 1000 seeds).

What it doesn't show: This does not prove that real sunflowers are built by this calculation. The model only looks at which angle fills a disc evenly in geometry; for real plants there is an explanation in which new seeds form in the emptiest spot between existing ones (hormones and inhibition), and the angle follows from that. Also, the golden angle is not the only one that fills well: with 600 seeds, 73% of the angles had an average gap below 0.5. The measured result is that the golden angle is among the lowest and most even of them.

Inspired by the spiral arrangement in Vogel (1979), "A better way to construct the sunflower head", Mathematical Biosciences 44, and by Douady and Couder (1992), "Phyllotaxis as a physical self-organized growth process", Physical Review Letters 68. This implementation is a geometric model that computes positions; it does not reproduce the numbers of either paper.
Packing quality uses probe points spaced 0.35 times the ideal spacing inside 85% of the disc radius, measuring the distance to the nearest seed. Seed k sits at radius √(k+0.5).

Measuring 90° to 180° in 0.1° steps (901 angles), the coefficient of variation of neighbor distances was slightly lower at 99.5° (the same value as another golden-ratio angle, 360°/(φ+2)) at 0.011 than at the golden angle (0.012), and every other angle was higher. You can verify with node tools/validate-sunflower.js.
The code is available on GitHub.
Is Success Talent or Luck? · Simulatio Lab
Talent is bell-shaped, so why does wealth pile up in a few hands? Run the Talent vs Luck simulation yourself by changing the variables.
Talent clusters around the average, yet wealth and success pile up extremely at the top. We check with a model in which 1,000 people meet lucky and unlucky events over 40 years.
1,000 people get talent from a normal distribution (mean 0.6, SD 0.1), and everyone starts with the same capital (10).
Across the screen, 500 lucky and unlucky points move randomly every 6 months.
When a lucky point passes, capital doubles with probability equal to talent. When an unlucky point passes, capital is halved regardless of talent.
